statement: A stand-alone notice is shown before or together with every consent request. The notice lists the personal data collected, the purposes and what each purpose enables, how to withdraw consent and use rights, and how to complain to the Board. Each collection point is reviewed whenever it is added or changed, so that people can give informed consent. The approved notice and the consent screens are the proof.
why_asked: If the notice sits only in a site footer or depends on other documents, people consent without knowing what they agree to. Consultants should check the notice at the moment of the request, not just that a privacy page exists.
how_to_ask: Walk through each place where consent is collected, on the web, in the app and on paper, and look at what the person sees first. Check that the notice can be understood without opening anything else. Example probe: "Show me the sign-up screen as a new customer sees it. Where is the notice, and does it say how to complain to the Board?"
question: Does your organization show a stand-alone notice before or with every consent request that explains the data, the purposes, the rights and the complaint route?
expected_evidence: Privacy notice; screenshots or recordings of every consent collection flow; list of consent collection points; notice approval record; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: Every collection point presents a notice before or with the consent request. The notice itemizes the personal data, states each purpose and what it enables, explains how to withdraw consent and exercise rights, and explains how to complain to the Board. It makes sense on its own and is reviewed when a collection point changes.
test: List all consent collection points and sample a mix of channels, at least one web and one app or paper flow where they exist. For each, check the notice appears before or with the request and covers the data, purposes, withdrawal and rights route, and the Board complaint route. Pass if every sampled flow meets all points and the notice is readable without other documents.
baseline_risk: People give consent without knowing what data is taken or why, and consent given on that basis is open to challenge.

statement: Every notice and consent request can be read in English or in the person's choice of another officially listed language. The language options and their translations are kept current whenever a notice or consent screen changes. This lets people understand what they agree to in a language they use. The language selector and the translated texts are the proof.
why_asked: A notice that people cannot read in their own language does not make their consent informed. Consultants should look for a working language choice, not only a translated policy page.
how_to_ask: Ask which languages are offered and how a person picks one at the consent screen. Ask who keeps translations aligned when the English text changes. Example probe: "Open the consent screen and switch it to Hindi. Does the notice change as well, or only the button labels?"
question: Does your organization offer each notice and consent request in English or in the person's choice of another officially listed language?
expected_evidence: Language selector screenshots for each consent flow; translated notice and consent texts; translation review or approval record; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: Each consent flow offers English and a choice of officially listed languages at the point of the request. Translations of the notice and the consent text match the current English text. Someone owns translation updates when wording changes.
test: Select a sample of consent flows and open each in English and in at least one other listed language. Check that both the notice and the consent text appear in the chosen language and match the current English wording. Pass if every sampled flow offers the choice and the translations are complete and current.
baseline_risk: People who do not read English cannot give informed consent, and the organization cannot show that its consent is valid for them.

statement: The people whose personal data was collected before the organization's current privacy duties began are identified. A notice is then sent to them as soon as reasonably practicable, describing the personal data held and the purposes it is used for. This brings older data under the same transparency as new data. The list of affected people, the notice and the dispatch log are the proof.
why_asked: Data collected years ago often carries no notice and no clear consent. Consultants should check that the organization found this older population and actually contacted it, rather than assuming it is covered.
how_to_ask: Ask how the organization identified data collected before its current duties and how many people are affected. Ask to see the notice and the record of sending it. Example probe: "How did you find customers whose data you held before this program started, and when did their notices go out?"
question: Has your organization sent a notice to people whose personal data was collected before its current privacy duties began?
expected_evidence: Register or extract of people with older consented data; retrospective notice text; dispatch log with dates and channels; plan or schedule for remaining recipients; covering the period since the duties began.
good_looks_like: The organization has identified the people whose data predates its current duties. A notice describing the data held and its purposes has been sent through suitable channels, with dates recorded. Anyone not yet reached is on a dated plan.
test: Obtain the list of people with older data and check how it was built. Sample recipients and trace each to a dispatch record showing date and channel. Check the notice text describes the data held and the purposes. Pass if the population is identified, the sampled recipients were notified, and the notice content is complete.
baseline_risk: Older data is held and used with no notice, so the organization cannot show that people were told what it holds about them.
applicability: Applies if the organization holds personal data collected before its current privacy duties began.

statement: The contact details of the person who answers privacy questions appear in every notice and are shown prominently on the website and app. The details are checked whenever the contact person changes. This gives people a working route for questions about their data. The published pages and the notices are the proof.
why_asked: A privacy contact that is missing, out of date or hidden leaves people with nobody to ask, and requests stall. Consultants should test that the contact is findable and reaches a real person.
how_to_ask: Look for the contact on the home page, in the app and in the notice shown at consent. Then test it. Example probe: "Show me where a customer finds the privacy contact in your app, then send a test message and show me who receives it."
question: Does your organization publish the contact details of the person who answers privacy questions in its notices and prominently on its website or app?
expected_evidence: Website and app screenshots showing the contact; current notice text; role or appointment record naming the contact person; sample responses to people's requests showing the contact; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: The contact details of a named role or person appear in each notice and in a prominent place on the website and app. The details are current and the mailbox or channel is monitored. Responses to people also carry the contact.
test: Check the website, the app and the notice at each consent flow for the contact details. Send a test message to the published channel and confirm it reaches the named person. Sample responses to people's requests from the review period and check they include the contact. Pass if the contact is present, prominent, current and reachable.
baseline_risk: People cannot reach anyone about their data, questions turn into complaints, and the organization cannot show it gave a working contact.

statement: Consent is collected only through a clear affirmative action by the person. Screens carry no pre-selected options, never treat silence or continued use as consent, and show accept and decline with equal prominence. Each consent flow is reviewed when it is built or changed. This keeps consent real and not manufactured by design. The approved consent designs and live screen captures are the proof.
why_asked: Pre-ticked boxes and nudging screens produce consent that people never really gave. Consultants should look at the live screens, not only the approved designs.
how_to_ask: Ask for the design standard for consent screens, then open the live flows. Check defaults, button emphasis and any wording that pushes toward accepting. Example probe: "Open the sign-up flow. Is any box already ticked, and is the decline button as easy to see as accept?"
question: Does your organization collect consent only through a clear affirmative action by the person, without pre-selected options, silence, continued use or manipulative design?
expected_evidence: Consent screen design standard; dated screenshots or recordings of every live consent flow; design approval records; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: Every consent request needs an affirmative action such as an unticked box or a clear button. No option is pre-selected, silence or continued use is never counted, and accept and decline look equally prominent. Live screens match the approved designs.
test: Capture or obtain dated screens for a sample of consent flows from the review period, covering each channel. Check there is an affirmative action, no pre-selected choice, no consent inferred from inactivity or continued use, and equal prominence for accept and decline. Pass if every sampled flow meets all points and matches the approved design.
baseline_risk: Consent is collected through defaults or pressure, so it is not valid and any processing based on it is exposed.

statement: Consent is given freely. The service does not make access depend on consent to processing it does not need, and no consent request contains a term by which people waive their rights. Sign-up flows and linked terms are checked whenever they change. This stops people from being forced to trade away their data or rights. The consent screens, the terms and a decline walkthrough are the proof.
why_asked: Bundling optional processing into the core service, or burying a waiver in the terms, makes consent coerced. Consultants should test what happens when a person says no.
how_to_ask: Ask which processing is needed to deliver the service and which is optional. Then ask for a sign-up that declines every optional item. Example probe: "If I decline marketing and analytics at sign-up, do I still get the full service?"
question: Does your organization keep consent free by not making access to a service depend on processing the service does not need?
expected_evidence: List of processing needed for each service and optional processing; consent screens; terms of service and terms linked from consent flows; recorded sign-up walkthrough declining optional items; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: The organization has decided which processing each service needs and treats the rest as optional. A person can decline every optional item and still reach the core service. No terms linked from consent flows waive a right or allow processing the law forbids.
test: Select a sample of services and run a sign-up that declines every optional purpose. Check the sign-up completes and the core service works. Read the terms linked from the consent flows for any waiver of rights. Pass if every sampled sign-up completes without optional consent and no waiver term is found.
baseline_risk: People are forced to accept unneeded processing or give up their rights to use a service, and the resulting consent is not valid.

statement: Every consent request states the specific purpose in clear and plain language, so that the person knows what they agree to. The wording of each request is reviewed when it is written or changed. This makes consent informed and not generic. The approved consent texts and live screens are the proof.
why_asked: Vague purposes such as "improve our services" make consent uninformed. Consultants should read the actual wording a person sees.
how_to_ask: Collect the consent text from each flow and read it as a customer would. Check each purpose is specific and the language is plain. Example probe: "Read me the sentence that explains why you collect the phone number. Would a first-time user understand it?"
question: Does your organization state the specific purpose, in clear and plain language, in every consent request?
expected_evidence: Consent request texts for every flow; wording review or approval records; dated screenshots of live consent screens; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: Each consent request names the specific purpose in short, plain sentences with no legal or technical jargon. The wording is reviewed before release and live screens match the approved text.
test: Sample consent requests across channels from the review period. For each, check a specific purpose is named and the wording is plain and understandable without other documents. Pass if every sampled request states a specific purpose in plain language.
baseline_risk: People consent to purposes they do not understand, so the consent is not informed and cannot be relied on.

statement: Each purpose appears as a separate item in the consent request, and the person can give or withhold consent for each one. A separate unticked control is built for every optional purpose. Refusing or withdrawing one purpose leaves the others unchanged. This allows real partial consent. The consent screens and the stored consent states are the proof.
why_asked: A single combined consent forces all-or-nothing choices and hides purposes. Consultants should check that the choice works in the system, not only on the screen.
how_to_ask: Open a flow that serves more than one purpose and ask to switch one purpose off. Then look at what the system does with it. Example probe: "Turn off the marketing purpose but keep the service purpose. What changes in the system?"
question: Does your organization list each purpose separately in the consent request and let people give or withhold consent for each one?
expected_evidence: Consent screens for flows with more than one purpose; design of per-purpose controls; consent log extract showing per-purpose states; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: Where data serves more than one purpose, each purpose is its own item with its own unticked control. The notice describes the data used for each purpose. People with mixed choices exist in the records and the system respects them.
test: Select consent flows that serve more than one purpose. For each, check purposes are listed separately with separate unticked controls. Test one partial choice and confirm the other purposes are unaffected. Check the consent log holds people with mixed per-purpose states. Pass if every sampled flow offers separate choices and partial consent works.
baseline_risk: People cannot refuse some purposes while accepting others, so consent is bundled and not specific.

statement: Auditable consent records are kept. Each record shows the purpose, the date and time, the capture channel, the notice version shown, and any later withdrawal, stored separately for each purpose. The records are protected from alteration. This lets the organization prove consent when asked. The consent log and the notice archive are the proof.
why_asked: Without records the organization cannot show who agreed to what, and a challenge becomes its word against the person's. Consultants should ask to see one person's full consent history.
how_to_ask: Pick a person and ask for everything the organization holds about their consent. Check the notice shown can also be produced. Example probe: "For this customer, show me when they consented, to which purposes, through which channel and which notice they saw."
question: Does your organization keep auditable records of when, how and for which purpose each person gave consent?
expected_evidence: Consent log schema; consent log extract for a sample of people; notice version archive; withdrawal records; access control or change history for the log; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: Each record holds the purpose, timestamp, channel and notice version, with a separate status for each purpose and every withdrawal logged. Records cannot be changed without trace. The matching notice version can be produced for any person.
test: Select a sample of people across channels and ask for their consent records. Check each shows the purpose, date and time, channel, notice version and any withdrawal, with a separate status per purpose. Ask for the matching notice version for each. Pass if all sampled records are complete and every notice version is produced.
baseline_risk: The organization cannot prove consent was given, so any processing based on it is hard to defend.

statement: A trigger ensures that any new or changed purpose is reviewed before processing starts. Fresh notice and consent for that purpose are collected before the new processing begins. Existing consent is never reused for a purpose it did not cover. This keeps processing within what people agreed to. The change procedure and the new consent records are the proof.
why_asked: Teams often reuse data for a new feature on the strength of old consent. Consultants should look for a gate that stops this and for proof it worked on a real change.
how_to_ask: Ask how a new use of data is brought to those who handle privacy and what stops it going live without consent. Then ask for a recent example. Example probe: "Tell me about the last new feature that used existing data in a new way. When was consent collected relative to launch?"
question: Does your organization obtain fresh consent before processing personal data for a new or changed purpose?
expected_evidence: Change procedure with the privacy trigger; product or purpose change records; consent log extract showing new consent dates; launch dates for the new processing; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: A documented step requires privacy review of every new or changed purpose before launch. Fresh notice and consent are collected first, and consent records are dated before the processing started. Old consent is not stretched to cover new uses.
test: List new or changed purposes introduced in the review period and sample them. For each, compare the consent record date with the launch date of the new processing. Pass if every sampled purpose has fresh consent dated before the processing began, and the change procedure contains the trigger.
baseline_risk: Data is reused for purposes people never agreed to, which makes the new processing unlawful.

statement: People can withdraw consent as easily as they gave it. Withdrawal takes no more steps and no less accessible a channel than giving consent, and the notice says how to do it. Give and withdraw flows are checked side by side whenever either changes. This keeps withdrawal from becoming a hurdle. The side-by-side flows are the proof.
why_asked: If giving consent takes one tap and withdrawing takes a letter, the right to withdraw is hollow. Consultants should compare the two paths directly.
how_to_ask: Ask the client to demonstrate giving consent and then withdrawing it in each channel, and count the steps. Example probe: "Consent was given in the app with two taps. Show me how long it takes to withdraw it in the app."
question: Does your organization let people withdraw consent as easily as they gave it?
expected_evidence: Side-by-side recordings or screenshots of the give and withdraw flows in each channel; notice text on how to withdraw; counts of steps for each flow; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: In every channel, withdrawal takes no more steps than giving consent and uses the same kind of channel. Consent given in the app can be withdrawn in the app. The notice tells people where to withdraw.
test: Select a sample of consent flows across channels and run the give and the withdraw path for each. Count steps and compare the channels. Check the notice explains how to withdraw. Pass if withdrawal takes no more steps and no less accessible a channel than giving consent in every sampled flow.
baseline_risk: People are discouraged or blocked from withdrawing consent, and the organization keeps processing on consent people no longer want to give.

statement: Processing stops, and processors are made to stop, within a defined period after consent is withdrawn. The exception is processing the law requires or allows without consent. Stop instructions to processors are issued and recorded. This makes withdrawal have a real effect. The withdrawal log and the processor instruction records are the proof.
why_asked: A withdrawal button that changes nothing behind the scenes is worse than none. Consultants should trace a withdrawal through to the systems and the processors.
how_to_ask: Ask for a documented withdrawal procedure and the period it sets. Then pick a withdrawal and trace what stopped and when, including at processors. Example probe: "Take a withdrawal from last month. Show me the date processing stopped in your system and at your email vendor."
question: Does your organization stop processing, and make its processors stop, within a defined period after a person withdraws consent?
expected_evidence: Withdrawal procedure stating the period; withdrawal log; processor instruction records and confirmations; records of retention grounds where the law requires keeping data; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: A written procedure sets the period for stopping processing after withdrawal and requires processors to stop too. Each withdrawal is logged with the date processing stopped, including at processors. Any data kept because the law requires it has a recorded ground.
test: Sample withdrawals from the review period. For each, check the date of withdrawal, the date processing stopped in internal systems and the processor stop instruction and confirmation. Pass if every sampled withdrawal was applied within the defined period, including at processors, or has a recorded legal ground for keeping the data.
baseline_risk: Processing continues after people withdraw consent, which is unlawful and erodes trust.

statement: Consent actions are accepted through an intermediary only where the intermediary is a consent manager on the Board's published list. The organization's systems treat consent given, reviewed or withdrawn through the intermediary the same as direct actions. The intermediary's records are reconciled with internal consent status on a regular cycle. The agreement, the register extract and the reconciliation are the proof.
why_asked: An unlisted intermediary may not be trusted to speak for people, and a withdrawal made there that is never applied leaves processing running without consent. Consultants should check both the registration and the data flow.
how_to_ask: First ask whether any intermediary sends consent actions. If so, check each against the Board's published list, then follow one withdrawal into the internal system. Example probe: "Show me this consent manager on the Board's list, and a withdrawal that came through it and where it shows in your consent log."
question: If your organization accepts consent through consent managers, does it accept only consent managers on the Board's published list and apply their actions as it would direct ones?
expected_evidence: Agreements with each consent manager; extract of the Board's published list showing each one; integration documentation; reconciliation of consent manager records against the internal consent log; covering the review period.
good_looks_like: Each intermediary is checked against the Board's published list before it is used and the check is recorded. Consent, review and withdrawal through it update the internal consent status in the same way as direct actions. Reconciliations show no unapplied withdrawals.
test: List every consent manager in use and check each against the Board's published list. Sample people from the review period and compare the manager's consent and withdrawal records with the internal consent log. Pass if every manager is listed and every sampled action, especially withdrawals, was applied internally.
baseline_risk: Consent actions arrive through unlisted or unreliable channels, and withdrawals made there are never applied.
applicability: Applies if the organization accepts consent actions through consent managers.
